title: Is a hair transplant permissible in Islam?
headline: Fatwas allow hair transplants to restore lost hair and forbid them for adornment

summary.text: Contemporary fatwas generally permit hair transplantation when it restores hair lost through illness, injury, or a genuine defect, and prohibit it when done purely for adornment. The four schools' classical books address wasl (hair-joining), not transplantation, so each school's position on transplants is a modern extension of its stated rule. The International Islamic Fiqh Academy listed hair transplants for hair loss, especially for women, among permitted procedures.

paragraphs.text: The verse central to the discussion is Satan's vow in Surat al-Nisa: "And I will mislead them, and I will arouse in them [sinful] desires, and I will command them so they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will command them so they will change the creation of Allāh" (Quran 4:119). The tafsir describes Satan's misguidance as having two main strands: superstition and interference in God's creation. When Ibn Mas'ud cursed women who tattoo, pluck and file teeth "changing the creation of Allah," Umm Ya'qub objected that she had read the whole Quran and found no such thing; he answered by reciting, "And whatever the Messenger has given you, take; and what he has forbidden you, refrain from" (Quran 59:7), then said, "Then he did forbid it".

A second verse, "No change should there be in the creation of Allāh" (Quran 30:30), is read by the tafsir as referring to the fitrah, the religion upon which people were created, rather than to bodily surgery. That distinction matters because it shows the Companions did not treat every physical alteration as a violation of the verse.

The prohibition texts are sound and agreed upon, and they concern wasl, attaching hair to hair. "Allah has cursed the woman who adds hair extensions and the woman who has them added" (Sahih al-Bukhari 5941). The same meaning comes from Asma' bint Abi Bakr (Sahih al-Bukhari 5941, Sahih Muslim 2122c, 2123a–b, Sunan Ibn Majah 1988, all graded sahih), and from Aisha in Sahih al-Bukhari 5205.

Two details in these narrations carry the weight of the whole debate. First, the woman's daughter had lost her hair to measles and had just married, and the Prophet ﷺ still refused, in one wording, "Her husband has ordered me to join extra hair to her hair." He said, "No. Those women who join hair (to other women's hair) have been cursed". Second, Ibn Abbas's narration adds the qualifier "when it is not for an illness" (min ghayri dā'), graded sahih by al-Albani and Muhammad Muhyi al-Din Abd al-Hamid but da'if by Zubair Ali Zai, and this qualifier is what later jurists built the treatment exception on.

Mu'awiya, on the pulpit in Madinah, took a lock of hair from a guard's hand and said he had heard the Prophet ﷺ forbid the like of it and call it al-zūr, falsehood; the narration is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. Ibn Mas'ud's version, with the phrase "changing the creation of Allah," is in Sahih al-Bukhari 4886 and 5943 and elsewhere. He also personally refused a woman with sparse hair who asked to add extensions, saying he had heard it from the Messenger ﷺ (Sunan an-Nasa'i 5098, graded sahih).

On the permitting side stand two hadith. The first is the story of the three men of the Children of Israel, including the bald man: "He said: 'Good hair, and to get rid of what makes me disgusting in the eyes of people.' He wiped over his head, so his condition went away and he was given good hair" (Sahih al-Bukhari 3464, also Sahih Muslim 2964). Ibn Uthaymeen used this to argue that restoring lost hair is a return of what Allah created, not an addition to it. The second is, "Allah has not sent down any disease except that He has also sent down a cure for it" (Sunan Ibn Majah 3439, graded sahih), alongside the maxim "There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm" (Sunan Ibn Majah 2341, graded sahih by al-Albani and da'if by Zubair Ali Zai).

The Hanafi book Al-Ikhtiyar states that joining hair with human hair is haram, whether her own or another's, because of falsification (tazwīr) and because it uses a part of a human body. Ibn Abidin adds that al-Tatar Khaniyya calls joining with another's hair merely makruh, and that non-human hair was licensed, reported from Abu Yusuf. Hanafi muftis divide: some allow transplant of one's own follicles, or treat baldness as a defect to be removed; others allow it only with non-human or synthetic hair and forbid transplanting human hair, even one's own.

The Shafi'i book Mughni al-Muhtaj states that joining human hair to human hair, or joining with impure hair, is haram, since human hair and body parts may not be used, for the honour of the human being. Pure non-human hair is haram for an unmarried woman; for a married woman there are three views, the soundest being permissible with the husband's permission. A contemporary Shafi'i fatwa permits transplant of the head's own hair because "there is no deceit therein".

The Malikis did not differentiate between hair and other materials in the prohibition, holding wasl haram absolutely since the hadiths are general; coloured threads and the like used as ornament are permitted. Qadi Iyad and al-Nafrawi in al-Fawakih al-Dawani hold that merely placing hair on the head without joining it is permitted, since it is like woollen or silk braids. A transplant, which grows from the scalp rather than being attached, is argued to fall outside wasl on this reading.

The Hanbali book Kashshaf al-Qina' states that joining hair with hair is haram even with animal hair and even with the husband's permission, because a curse indicates prohibition. Al-Mughni records Ahmad's prohibition of even qarāmil and wool. The same Hanbali text preserves al-Muwaffaq's counter-view: "what is prohibited is only joining hair with hair, because of the deception in it," and the reports are carried as makruh; non-hair may be used out of need.
The four schools agree that joining human hair to human hair is prohibited; they differ over non-human material, the husband's permission, and how broadly the curse is applied.

The apparent conflict is between a curse on joining hair and a permission to treat disease. Scholars resolved it along four lines. First, definition: wasl attaches foreign hair that hangs and adds length or bulk, creating a false appearance and never becoming part of the body; a transplant moves the person's own living follicles, which take root and grow, so it is closer to reattaching a severed finger than to adding hair. Those who reject even this reply that the hair is still displaced from where it grew.

Second, the operative cause: the Hanafis, Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis all name deception (tadlīs, tazwīr) as the reason for the ban, which is why the Prophet ﷺ called it al-zūr. Where no deception is intended or produced, the reason is absent.

Third, defect versus adornment: the qualifier "when it is not for an illness" in Ibn Abbas's narration, the hadith of the bald man given back good hair, and the command to seek treatment are read together to carve out restoration of a defect while leaving vanity under the prohibition. Ibn Uthaymeen's formula is that returning what was lost is not "adding to what Allah created".

Fourth, the hardest counter-evidence: the Ansari bride had lost her hair to measles, her husband wanted her to look good, and the Prophet ﷺ still said no. Scholars who permit transplants answer that she asked for wasl, added hair, not for the restoration of her own; scholars who refuse answer that if need and a husband's wish did not open the door there, cosmetic desire will not. Al-Albani took the second route explicitly.

The International Islamic Fiqh Academy, in its eighteenth session in Putrajaya (2007), resolution 173 (18/11), listed among permitted procedures "hair transplants in case of hair loss, especially for women," under correcting defects from burns, accidents and illness. Jordan's General Iftaa' Department reports the same resolution approvingly.

Ibn Baz distinguished purpose: if the surgery is for medical treatment it falls under treatment, while if it is for frivolity, adornment or imitating the enemies of Allah it does not. Ibn Uthaymeen is reported in two directions: the fatwa collection Fatawa Ulama al-Balad al-Haram has him permitting it as "returning what Allah created" and removing a defect, not beautification, while in his explanation of Bulugh al-Maram he says he holds back from it because of the curse on the joiner and the joined, and that the loss of hair does not harm a person of vitality.

Among the Hanafis, Ebrahim Desai permits it where baldness causes psychological or social difficulty, calling baldness a defect that treatment may remove, and permits moving one's own hair from the back of the head to the front; Darul Iftaa Chicago permits it if the implanted hair is synthetic or from the patient's own body; Darul Uloom Deoband and Muftionline permit it only where the hair used is not human. Islamweb permits it with one's own or another's hair, preferring one's own; Nasser Farid Wasel, former Mufti of Egypt, permits it from the woman's own body but restricts another person's hair to necessity; al-Albani, asked about a man who lost all his hair and wore a wig, called it the strongest form of wasl and said it is not permissible; the Assembly of Muslim Jurists of America answered a question on non-human hairpieces by stating that joining a woman's hair with anything that resembles hair is haram.

Two practical points recur in the fatwas: hair that grows from a transplant takes the ruling of natural hair for wudu and ghusl, whereas glued or bonded hair that water cannot reach is a separate problem; and where another person's hair is used, the Hanafi and Shafi'i books object that human parts may not be used at all, while others see no difference between one's own follicles and another's.
